topic: Imu's power runs entirely through borrowed bodies (the Empty Throne, Gunko, Harald, York) and that dependency is a real weakness
title: Why Imu Never Leaves That Throne
description:
Imu has never thrown a punch, cast a spell, or walked into a fight in Imu's own body. Every confirmed Imu action, from killing Nefertari Cobra to possessing Gunko in Elbaph, runs through someone else. Here's the theory: that dependency is the one crack this villain has always had.

0:38 The Empty Throne
2:32 Borrowed Bodies
4:55 What The Knights Prove
6:48 The Steelman
8:27 The One Crack
10:30 The Verdict
comment: If Imu needs a borrowed body just to act, does that make Imu beatable, or just more dangerous? Pick a side.

lines.text: Imu has sat on the Empty Throne since chapter 908, and I don't think that's a show of strength.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler seated on an ancient throne

lines.text: I think it's the only way Imu gets to act in this story at all.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure on a throne

lines.text: So here's the question: what if the strongest villain in One Piece can't actually move without borrowing something first?

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler watching from a throne

lines.text: Every confirmed Imu action so far has one detail in common nobody talks about.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler issuing a command

lines.text: Imu never swings a fist. Imu never draws a blade. Imu lets the throne do the terrifying part...

shot.fallback: ruler sitting perfectly still

lines.text: In chapter 1085, Imu kills Nefertari Cobra, then calmly climbs down from that very throne.

shot.fallback: ruler striking down a king from a seated position

lines.text: Right now, in Elbaph, Imu isn't even wearing Imu's own body.

shot.fallback: controlled soldier moving with someone else's will

lines.text: Imu is riding inside Gunko, a soldier who wasn't even on this side a few chapters ago...

shot.fallback: soldier with glowing, controlled eyes

lines.text: A god who needs a throne to kill from and a stranger's body to fight in isn't my idea of all-powerful.

shot.fallback: controlled warrior moving toward a target

lines.text: Start with the throne itself, because it's the first thing we ever actually see Imu do...

shot.fallback: ancient throne room at a world summit

lines.text: Chapter 908 introduces the Empty Throne at the Reverie, a seat every Gorosei answers to above even the Five Elders' own authority.

shot.fallback: five elders bowing before an empty seat

lines.text: Every single world leader at that Reverie, kings and queens included, bows to a chair they're told has nobody in it.

shot.fallback: world leaders bowing before a vacant seat

lines.text: For years, Oda let readers assume that throne was symbolic, a seat of law with nobody actually in it.

shot.fallback: grand throne room, vacant seat

lines.text: Then chapter 1085 happens, and the throne isn't empty. It was never empty.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure revealed on a throne

lines.text: Imu was sitting there through everything: the Reverie, Marineford's aftermath, Luffy's entire rise to Emperor.

shot.fallback: ruler observing world events from a throne

lines.text: And Imu still hasn't fought anyone with Imu's own two hands, not once, not even now.

shot.fallback: ruler remaining seated through conflict

lines.text: Compare that to every other major villain in this story, and the gap gets obvious fast.

shot.fallback: lineup of powerful antagonists

lines.text: Kaido flew across Onigashima on his own dragon body. Big Mom walked into Totto Land's streets herself.

shot.fallback: dragon warlord and giant empress fighting directly

lines.text: Blackbeard boarded Marineford personally to take Whitebeard's final prize with his own hands.

shot.fallback: dark pirate captain fighting on a battlefield

lines.text: Even the Gorosei themselves showed up on Egghead in their own bodies to fight Luffy's crew directly.

shot.fallback: five elders engaging in direct combat

lines.text: Every one of them shows up eventually. Imu has never shown up anywhere, not once, not as Imu.

shot.fallback: empty space where a ruler should stand

lines.text: That's not restraint. I think that's a limit Oda built in from the very first page Imu appeared on.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure constrained by unseen rules

lines.text: Think about the sheer size of the government built around that one chair: five Elders, an admiralty, an entire army of Celestial Dragons.

shot.fallback: vast government structure surrounding a throne

lines.text: That's not the architecture of a being who can simply walk anywhere unchallenged. That's the architecture of something being protected.

shot.fallback: layered defenses around a single seat

lines.text: Every layer of that government exists to keep ordinary people as far from the throne room as possible, generation after generation.

shot.fallback: guarded gates leading toward a distant throne

lines.text: Here's a detail most recaps skip entirely: Imu was shocked, visibly, when Joy Boy's attack landed in chapter 1122.

shot.search: Imu Joy Boy attack shock chapter 1122
shot.fallback: shadowy ruler reacting with genuine shock

lines.text: Would a being with zero limits really flinch at a memory six hundred years old resurfacing out of nowhere?

shot.fallback: ruler recoiling from an old memory

lines.text: A being running its power through something borrowed absolutely would, because the connection itself can be hit...

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler dependent on a vessel

lines.text: So that's rule one, straight from the page: the throne is the only body Oda has ever confirmed Imu personally keeps...

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler bound to a single seat

lines.text: Now here's rule two, and Elbaph is proving it in real time this exact week.

shot.fallback: giant battlefield under a darkened sky

lines.text: Chapter 1193 confirms Imu possessing Gunko to use Domi Reversi against the giants defending Harald.

shot.fallback: controlled soldier casting a dark technique

lines.text: Domi Reversi isn't Imu's own trick, either. It's a power Imu is channeling through someone else's body.

shot.fallback: glowing technique channeled through a possessed body

lines.text: Think about how strange that is. The most feared figure in this world needs a borrowed body just to cast one spell.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler dependent on a vessel to act

lines.text: Community threads on this arc keep circling the same question: does Imu get weaker if a host resists or dies?

shot.fallback: controlled warrior struggling against control

lines.text: Nobody's answered that on-panel yet. But the setup only makes sense if the answer ends up being yes.

shot.fallback: ruler reacting to a lost connection

lines.text: Because if hosts cost Imu nothing at all, Oda wouldn't keep drawing Imu reaching for new ones every arc.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure extending control toward a new target

lines.text: Harald, Elbaph's own king, was reportedly taking orders from Imu before Loki ever stepped in to stop it.

shot.fallback: giant king kneeling before a shadowy ruler

lines.text: That's a second vessel in this exact arc, on top of Gunko, on top of the throne itself.

shot.fallback: three separate figures linked to one controlling force

lines.text: A ruler who needs this many stand-ins to run one single battlefield is not running on unlimited power.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler straining to control multiple bodies

lines.text: To understand why Imu needs vessels at all, go back to what the Void Century actually buried.

shot.fallback: ancient ruins hinting at a hidden past

lines.text: Ohara's scholars died trying to read Poneglyphs that Imu's own order made illegal to study anywhere.

shot.fallback: burning library island

lines.text: Robin's research, carried since she was a child, keeps circling one idea: the Void Century erased a true history, not a small one.

shot.fallback: archaeologist reading ancient records

lines.text: If Imu rewrote the Poneglyphs, the Red Line, and a century of recorded history, that takes centuries of reach, not one lifetime of strength.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure overseeing centuries of history

lines.text: Reach across centuries, moving through other people's hands, is exactly what a vessel-based power looks like from the outside.

shot.fallback: shadowy influence spanning generations

lines.text: Vegapunk's own Punk Records on Egghead back this up in a smaller, more recent way.

shot.fallback: scientist reading ancient research archives

lines.text: York, one of Vegapunk's own satellites, had been quietly feeding secrets to the Gorosei long before Egghead ever started.

shot.fallback: robotic scientist secretly relaying information

lines.text: Imu's reach into Egghead wasn't a direct strike, either. It was one more borrowed set of hands, this time York's...

shot.fallback: shadowy influence working through a hidden informant

lines.text: So if one loyal satellite can be a hidden vessel for years without anybody noticing, how many more are out there right now?

shot.fallback: shadowy figures hiding in plain sight across the world

lines.text: York didn't need to be possessed, either. York simply chose to feed the Gorosei secrets, which is its own kind of vessel.

shot.fallback: robotic scientist serving a hidden master for decades

lines.text: A possessed body and a willing informant do the exact same job for Imu: a hand in the world Imu never has to risk.

shot.fallback: two different figures serving the same hidden purpose

lines.text: Willing or forced, it doesn't matter to the pattern. Both still count as a vessel standing between Imu and the consequences.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure shielded by a proxy

lines.text: That's three separate arcs now, three separate vessels, one unchanging pattern underneath every single one of them.

shot.fallback: three linked figures tracing back to one source

lines.text: Three vessels, three different arcs, and Imu never once needed to be seen doing any of it personally.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler staying hidden across multiple events

lines.text: Every one of these threads points the same direction: Imu's empire runs on people who can, in theory, stop cooperating...

shot.fallback: shadowy empire built on fragile loyalty

lines.text: That's the throne. That's Gunko. That's Harald. That's York. Always someone else, never Imu directly...

shot.fallback: multiple figures linked to one shadowy source

lines.text: Now let's look at the one place in this entire arc where Oda shows that power actually failing.

shot.search: Knights of God Imu power limits
shot.fallback: armored knights standing before a throne

lines.text: Knights of God are the clearest proof Imu doesn't just hand out strength for free to anyone.

shot.fallback: four knights in white cloaks

lines.text: Shepherd Sommers regenerates from almost anything Zoro throws at him across chapters 1193 and 1194.

shot.fallback: flesh knitting back together mid battle

lines.text: But that regeneration isn't unlimited, either. Sommers himself reveals Omen as the one real counter to Supreme King Haki.

shot.fallback: knight explaining calmly to an opponent

lines.text: If the Five Elders had to build a specific countermeasure into their own knights, Supreme King Haki was never something Imu could simply out-rule.

shot.fallback: cloaked elders designing a counter weapon

lines.text: Gaban figured out enough of this to coach Zoro toward it from the outside, without ever naming Imu once.

shot.fallback: old warrior advising a swordsman from a distance

lines.text: A retired fighter reading the Five Elders' own loophole faster than the knight using it says the system isn't as sealed as it looks.

shot.fallback: old warrior studying an enemy's weakness

lines.text: That's a loophole, written into the design on purpose. Gods don't need loopholes. Systems with limits do.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler constrained by rules

lines.text: Loopholes are exactly what a power running through pacts and proxies would need, chapter after chapter.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure managing scattered proxies

lines.text: It also explains why a Knight of God bothers talking at all instead of just finishing Zoro off clean.

shot.fallback: armored knight speaking calmly to stall

lines.text: Sommers isn't toying with Zoro for fun. Sommers is buying time for whatever pact is actually running him...

shot.fallback: knight stalling for a hidden purpose

lines.text: That reframes the entire fight. It's not strength versus strength. It's one proxy stalling until the real plan lands.

shot.fallback: two fighters locked in a stalling battle

lines.text: And the giants know something about pacts like this, even if they haven't said it to the Straw Hats yet.

shot.fallback: giant elders discussing an old secret

lines.text: Elbaph's own folklore is full of warnings about outsiders who ask for a king's word and never let go of it again.

shot.fallback: giant legends of binding oaths

lines.text: Those old stories always end the same way: the king who signs away one favor ends up owing everything.

shot.fallback: giant legend of a king's costly favor

lines.text: Harald's pact with Imu, whatever it actually cost him, follows that exact shape the giants already feared.

shot.fallback: giant king bound by an old agreement

lines.text: Loki's own hybrid dragon form might be the giants' answer to exactly this problem, a power that refuses to be borrowed.

shot.fallback: giant warrior transforming into a dragon form

lines.text: If Loki's strength can't be possessed the way Harald's loyalty was, that's not a coincidence Oda left lying around by accident...

shot.fallback: giant warrior radiating untouchable power

lines.text: That means Elbaph's royal family may have already proven a vessel can be reclaimed, months before Zoro ever lands a cut...

shot.fallback: giant royal family breaking free from outside control

lines.text: Now I want to steelman the obvious counter-argument here, because it's a genuinely strong one.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler facing a challenge

lines.text: Some fans argue Imu is simply immortal, full stop, maybe through a stolen Ope Ope no Mi, and doesn't need anyone.

shot.fallback: ruler untouched by time

lines.text: But immortality explains why Imu can't die. It doesn't explain why Imu keeps borrowing Gunko to throw one attack.

shot.fallback: controlled soldier casting an attack for a hidden master

lines.text: An immortal being with full personal power doesn't need a soldier's hands to cast Domi Reversi at all.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure casting power without a vessel

lines.text: It only needs those hands if something about acting directly is closed off, even to something that physically can't die.

shot.fallback: ruler blocked from acting directly

lines.text: So both theories can be true at once. Imu might be unkillable, and Imu might still be stuck working through other people...

shot.fallback: shadowy figure both eternal and constrained

lines.text: That combination is scarier than either theory alone, and here's exactly why I think that.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler looming over the world

lines.text: An immortal ruler with no limits at all is a wall you simply can't move, no matter what you try.

shot.fallback: immovable dark wall

lines.text: An immortal ruler who has to find a new vessel every time is a wall with a door built into it.

shot.fallback: wall with a hidden door

lines.text: And a door, even a small one, is the only thing a story like this has ever needed to end a villain.

shot.fallback: hero finding the one crack in a fortress

lines.text: Look at how every past untouchable villain in this story actually fell, one by one, across twenty years of chapters.

shot.fallback: fallen antagonists across the story

lines.text: Kaido wasn't beaten by raw power matching his own. Luffy found the one wound his scales couldn't cover.

shot.fallback: monkey warrior striking a dragon's weak point

lines.text: Doflamingo wasn't out-muscled, either. His own strings became the exact thing that trapped him in the end...

shot.fallback: puppet master caught in his own strings

lines.text: Oda's pattern is consistent across this entire series: the biggest threats fall to one specific exploit, never to brute force alone.

shot.fallback: hero exploiting a single flaw

lines.text: If Imu follows that same pattern, the exploit isn't going to be a bigger punch. It's going to be the vessel.

shot.fallback: hero striking at a controlled vessel instead of the master

lines.text: Here's what most theories about this exact fight get backwards, including a lot of the loud ones online.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler misread by onlookers

lines.text: People keep asking who's strong enough to beat Imu in a straight fight. But is that even the fight that matters?

shot.fallback: two warriors clashing pointlessly

lines.text: The fight that actually matters is whoever finally corners a vessel Imu can't walk away from in time.

shot.fallback: warrior cutting off a controlled soldier's escape

lines.text: That's not a weaker theory than raw power. It just answers a different question than the one everyone keeps asking.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler facing a reframed challenge

lines.text: And it lines up with something the Gorosei said at Egghead about protecting the throne above literally everything else.

shot.fallback: five elders guarding an empty seat

lines.text: Why guard a throne this hard if the thing sitting on it could simply walk away from any real danger?

shot.fallback: elders shielding a vulnerable seat

lines.text: You only build that much security around something that can actually be reached by someone determined enough.

shot.fallback: heavily guarded throne room

lines.text: So picture the version of this theory playing out in Elbaph specifically, right now, this exact week.

shot.fallback: battlefield under a watching shadow

lines.text: Gunko is already a soldier with her own will sitting underneath Imu's control, not a blank, empty puppet.

shot.fallback: soldier straining against outside control

lines.text: If Loki, or Zoro, or anyone on that battlefield forces Gunko to resist hard enough, something has to give.

shot.fallback: controlled soldier breaking free briefly

lines.text: Either Imu lets go and loses the vessel, or Imu holds on and pays a cost nobody has actually seen yet.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure straining to maintain control

lines.text: Both outcomes prove the exact same thing: Imu isn't simply unstoppable sitting behind Gunko's eyes.

shot.fallback: controlled soldier's eyes flickering with resistance

lines.text: That's a real crack, the first one this villain has ever actually shown us on the page...

shot.fallback: shadowy figure with a visible flaw

lines.text: Now take Harald's side of this same theory, because his story has been running in parallel the whole time.

shot.fallback: giant king caught between loyalties

lines.text: Harald reportedly took Imu's orders for years before Loki broke from his own father over exactly this.

shot.fallback: giant prince confronting his king father

lines.text: If Harald was ever a working vessel, and Loki's resistance helped sever that link, Elbaph already landed the first real hit on Imu's reach.

shot.fallback: giant warrior breaking a dark connection

lines.text: Nobody in the story has called it that yet, out loud. I think that's exactly what it actually was.

shot.fallback: giant warrior standing in quiet defiance

lines.text: It's worth remembering this isn't the first time a father figure's pact nearly cost a child everything, either.

shot.fallback: giant family history of broken trust

lines.text: Zoro's own arc runs the opposite direction: a mentor's lesson holding someone together instead of a king's pact pulling someone apart.

shot.fallback: swordsman and giant mirrored by contrast

lines.text: One Elbaph storyline is about control given away. The other is about control earned. Which one actually decides this arc?

shot.fallback: two parallel battles over control

lines.text: Which brings every thread of this theory back to one simple, testable idea, right here.

shot.fallback: threads converging on a single point

lines.text: Imu's power was never really about raw force. It's about how many hands Imu can borrow at once.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure extending influence through many hands

lines.text: Every vessel Imu uses is also, by definition, a vessel that can resist, break, or simply refuse the order.

shot.fallback: controlled figure wavering against control

lines.text: Cut off enough of them, and the throne stops being untouchable. It just becomes empty again, the way everyone always assumed it was...

shot.fallback: throne room slowly emptying of power

lines.text: People will say this makes Imu sound weak, and honestly, that's not what I'm arguing here.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler still looming large

lines.text: A being that can rewrite history through other people's hands for six hundred years is not weak by any real measure.

shot.search: Imu six hundred years power scale
shot.fallback: shadowy figure spanning centuries of history

lines.text: What I'm arguing is that this specific kind of power carries a specific kind of edge, one Oda has already shown us.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure with one visible limitation

lines.text: Fans who reject every Imu theory as unbeatable hype are skipping the one detail Oda keeps repeating on-panel.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler surrounded by doubt

lines.text: So which is it: is Imu untouchable, or just the best-hidden vessel user in the entire story?

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler framed by an open question

lines.text: It also answers a debate I keep seeing in the comments: is Imu really the final villain, or is someone above Imu too?

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler questioned by onlookers

lines.text: If Imu needs vessels to act, anyone above Imu needs the same thing, so that debate only has one real answer.

shot.fallback: layered hierarchy of shadowy figures

lines.text: Find the vessel, and you've found the leverage, no matter how many thrones sit behind the first one.

shot.fallback: hero identifying a vessel's leverage point

lines.text: Imu has never once acted in this story without something standing between Imu and the world outside that throne.

shot.fallback: shadowy figure always behind another figure

lines.text: Not at the Reverie. Not against Cobra. Not through York on Egghead. Not here in Elbaph. Not once...

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler repeating the same pattern

lines.text: So, does that make Imu's power a weakness, or just a different kind of strength nobody's learned to attack yet?

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler facing an uncertain future

lines.text: My honest verdict: it's both at once, and the next chapter to feature a struggling vessel is the one to watch for proof.

shot.fallback: battlefield anticipating a coming turn

lines.text: Watch what happens the next time a vessel actually fights back instead of just regenerating, obeying, or staying silent.

shot.fallback: controlled figure turning against control

lines.text: If Imu flinches even once when that happens, this stops being a theory and starts being confirmed.

shot.fallback: shadowy ruler showing a crack of weakness

lines.text: I've been wrong about this villain before, and I'd rather call the crack now than just repeat the hype everyone already has.

shot.fallback: narrator figure weighing a bold claim

lines.text: Tell me which vessel you think breaks first: Gunko, Harald, or something Oda hasn't even shown us yet.

shot.fallback: three possible weak points on a battlefield

lines.text: Whichever one it is, I don't think the Straw Hats beat Imu directly. I think they just outlast every hand Imu has left.

shot.fallback: pirate crew standing firm against a fading shadow

lines.text: And if you want to see what happens when someone's own control breaks instead of a villain's, that's the other story this channel told.

shot.fallback: swordsman standing at the edge of his limits
